prompt: Tenants receive random pairs from a shared worker fleet. A poisonous tenant crashes its two assigned workers. Another tenant shares one of those workers but has a healthy second worker. What determines whether that tenant continues serving?

options.text: Any shared worker means both tenants must be completely unavailable
options.explanation: Partial overlap need not remove every worker assigned to the second tenant.

options.text: Random assignment guarantees unchanged latency and throughput
options.explanation: The tenant has lost capacity; random assignment does not create spare resources.

options.text: It needs working rerouting or retries and enough capacity on its healthy worker
options.explanation: Correct. Shuffle sharding limits full overlap, but partial overlap can still degrade capacity and requires a usable surviving path.

options.text: It can freely retry on every worker in the global fleet
options.explanation: Ignoring the assigned subset can spread poison work and defeat isolation.

workedExample: Identify the actual subset that failed. The second tenant retains a worker, but that worker must accept the displaced traffic. Preserve the shard boundary, test retry/rerouting and reserve headroom; do not confuse a surviving worker with guaranteed service.

link.title: Workload isolation using shuffle-sharding (AWS Builders' Library)

prompt: A SaaS API is split into **20 cells**, each serving 5% of customers, behind a thin cell router. A bad config push and a poison-pill request both hit the same single cell. What is the blast radius, and what becomes the most important component to keep simple?

options.text: About 5% of customers; the cell router, because every request passes through it
options.explanation: Correct. One cell of 20 is 5% of customers. The router is shared by all cells, so it's the one place a bug hits everyone. Keep it thin, mostly static and changed rarely.

options.text: 100% of customers; cells only help with capacity
options.explanation: Cells are full, independent copies. A failure confined to one cell affects only the customers mapped to it.

options.text: About 5% of customers; the database in each cell, because it holds the data
options.explanation: Each cell's database only affects that cell. The shared component is the router.

options.text: About 50% of customers, since requests are retried in other cells
options.explanation: Cells don't normally retry customers' requests in other cells; doing so could spread a poison pill to every cell.

workedExample:
1. The prompt already states that the affected cell serves 5% of customers. A fault confined to it affects that slice.
2. The shared cell router and mapping remain on every request path.
3. Keep that router simple, use cached mappings where suitable, and stage its changes carefully.
4. Avoid cross-cell retries that spread poison work.
